The waterflea Pseudosida ramosa, a common cladoceran in tropical and subtropical freshwater systems, exhibits a characteristic life cycle whose early stages are closely tied to temperature. Newly released neonates, which emerge from the brood chamber after a brief period of embryonic development, measure approximately 0.075 cm [Lb = approximately 0.075 cm] in body length at birth. This small size, typical of many sidid cladocerans, marks the beginning of an exponential growth phase that is highly sensitive to thermal conditions. When maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the embryonic period—effectively the age at birth—lasts roughly 2.1 days [ab = roughly 2.1 days]. In contrast, elevating the water temperature to 30 °C [T = 30 °C] accelerates embryogenesis considerably, with neonates being released after approximately 1.4 days [ab = approximately 1.4 days]. This thermal sensitivity of early development is a key determinant of population dynamics, as it directly influences the interval between successive broods and the overall recruitment rate into the juvenile population. The initial body length at birth is a critical starting point for subsequent growth trajectories, which ultimately determine the size at which key life-history transitions, such as puberty and the attainment of maximum body size, occur. These early life-history events set the stage for the demographic performance of cohorts in fluctuating thermal environments.

Growth following the neonatal stage proceeds toward the attainment of reproductive competence. Individuals reach the total length at puberty of 0.16 cm [Lp = 0.16 cm], a modest size increase from the length at birth that nonetheless marks the onset of parthenogenetic reproduction typical of cladocerans. Under a rearing temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], one cohort study documented the time since birth at puberty as approximately 8.34 days [tp = approximately 8.34 days], while a second cohort study conducted under the same nominal temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] recorded a somewhat shorter time since birth at puberty of approximately 5.5 days [tp = approximately 5.5 days], illustrating the variability observed across independent laboratory trials.

Adults of Pseudosida ramosa ultimately attain a total length of 0.25 cm [Li = 0.25 cm], with a corresponding ultimate dry weight of approximately 0.00011 grams , a value scaled from the length-weight relationship established for the related cladoceran Ceriodaphnia dubia. This modest asymptotic body size is typical of small planktonic cladocerans that rely on rapid population turnover rather than large individual body size to persist in variable freshwater habitats.

Reproductive output in this species is pronounced and strongly temperature-dependent. At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 1.35 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 1.35 offspring per day], while at the warmer temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], this rate increases to approximately 3 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 3 offspring per day], reflecting the accelerating effect of temperature on reproductive turnover in this species. Longevity likewise varies with thermal regime: at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], one cohort study recorded a maximum lifespan of approximately 37.1 days [am = approximately 37.1 days], while a second cohort study under the same nominal temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] documented a considerably shorter maximum lifespan of approximately 14.8 days [am = approximately 14.8 days]. This variability across cohorts underscores the sensitivity of cladoceran life-history traits to subtle differences in rearing conditions and food availability between independent laboratory studies.
